Activated charcoal does not bind lithium, forced diuresis with furosemide increases lithium retention, and saline alone is too slow with an eGFR of 25.

It is not high-frequency oscillation, and evidence that it improves outcome in ARDS is limited.

It is especially useful when chest wall elastance is high (obesity, abdominal hypertension), where plateau pressure overestimates lung stress. oldText: VOO/DOO mode. Strongest distractor: It does not turn pacing off.
newText: Placing a magnet over most pacemakers closes a reed switch and changes the device to asynchronous pacing (VOO or DOO) at a fixed magnet rate (often 85–100/min, depending on the manufacturer and battery status). This prevents inhibition by electromagnetic interference, for example during diathermy, in pacing-dependent patients. Removing the magnet restores the programmed mode. It does not turn pacing off, and pacemakers have no defibrillator function. Effects vary between devices, so check with the device team when possible.

oldText: Used during diathermy. Strongest distractor: ICD magnet does not change pacing.
newText: On most ICDs, a magnet suspends tachyarrhythmia detection and therapy (shocks and anti-tachycardia pacing) for as long as it is in place, preventing inappropriate shocks from diathermy or during end-of-life care. Unlike on a pacemaker, the magnet does not change the bradycardia pacing mode, so a pacing-dependent patient with an ICD needs reprogramming to asynchronous pacing for surgery with monopolar diathermy. External defibrillation equipment must be available while therapies are suspended.

oldText: NBG code. Strongest distractor: Dual-chamber is DDD.
newText: The NBG pacemaker code describes the chamber paced (first letter), the chamber sensed (second) and the response to sensing (third: I inhibited, T triggered, D dual), with R for rate response. VVI paces the ventricle, senses the ventricle and inhibits pacing when an intrinsic ventricular beat is sensed, so it paces only when the rate falls below the set value. VOO paces the ventricle without sensing (asynchronous, as with a magnet), and DDD paces and senses both chambers with dual response, maintaining AV synchrony.

oldText: AV nodal blockers increase accessory pathway conduction. Strongest distractor: Procainamide is appropriate.
newText: In pre-excited AF (WPW), impulses can travel to the ventricles through the accessory pathway, which has a short refractory period, producing an irregular, very fast broad-complex tachycardia. AV nodal blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin, adenosine) slow nodal conduction, favour the accessory pathway and can precipitate VF, so they are contraindicated; ESC also advises against IV amiodarone. Unstable patients need synchronised cardioversion; stable patients can receive procainamide or ibutilide (or flecainide), and catheter ablation of the pathway follows.

oldText: Plus overdrive pacing or isoproterenol. Strongest distractor: Amiodarone prolongs QT.
newText: Torsades de pointes with QTc 560 ms is polymorphic VT associated with long QT. Give magnesium sulphate 2 g IV over 1–2 minutes (repeat or infusion) even if magnesium is normal, correct potassium (to 4.5–5.0 mmol/L) and stop QT-prolonging drugs. If torsades recurs, increase the heart rate to shorten the QT with overdrive pacing or isoprenaline (for acquired, pause-dependent torsades). Pulseless torsades is defibrillated. oldText: Treat urgently. Strongest distractor: Hypokalaemia shows U waves.
newText: ECG changes in hyperkalaemia progress roughly with potassium level: tall, narrow peaked T waves, then PR prolongation and flattening or loss of P waves, then QRS widening, and finally a sine-wave pattern, VF or asystole; the ECG is insensitive, and arrest can occur without warning. Any ECG change with hyperkalaemia needs immediate IV calcium. Hypokalaemia causes flat T waves, U waves and ST depression; hypercalcaemia shortens the QT; hypomagnesaemia is associated with QT prolongation and torsades.

oldText: Sinus tachycardia is commonest. Strongest distractor: Inferior MI shows ST elevation in II, III, aVF.
newText: In acute PE, the most common ECG finding is sinus tachycardia. Signs of right ventricular strain include the S1Q3T3 pattern (deep S in lead I, Q and inverted T in lead III), new right bundle branch block, right axis deviation, T-wave inversion in V1–V4 and atrial arrhythmias. These are insensitive (S1Q3T3 is present in under 20%) but, when present, point to a large PE and RV strain. Inferior MI produces ST elevation in II, III and aVF, pericarditis produces diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, and hyperkalaemia peaks the T waves.

oldText: Swinging heart. Strongest distractor: Hyperkalaemia gives peaked T.
newText: A large pericardial effusion lowers QRS voltage, and when the heart swings within the fluid each beat changes the electrical axis, producing electrical alternans (beat-to-beat changes in QRS amplitude). Sinus tachycardia, low voltage and alternans together strongly suggest tamponade, a clinical diagnosis (hypotension, raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus) supported by echo showing right atrial and ventricular diastolic collapse. Treat with urgent pericardiocentesis. Pneumothorax, obesity and emphysema lower voltage without alternans.

oldText: High-risk subendocardial ischaemia. Strongest distractor: Pericarditis shows aVR depression.
newText: ST elevation in aVR (often also V1) with widespread ST depression in six or more leads indicates diffuse subendocardial ischaemia, classically from left main or proximal three-vessel disease, but also from severe demand ischaemia (tachyarrhythmia, anaemia, hypotension) or after resuscitation. In the context of chest pain and instability, it calls for urgent angiography and haemodynamic support. Pericarditis typically produces PR elevation and ST depression in aVR with diffuse ST elevation, the reverse pattern.

oldText: Toxicity: bidirectional VT, AT with block. Strongest distractor: U waves indicate hypokalaemia.
newText: Digoxin effect, seen at therapeutic levels, produces down-sloping, scooped ('reverse tick' or Salvador Dali moustache) ST depression, a short QT, flattened or inverted T waves and sometimes prominent U waves; it does not mean toxicity. Digoxin toxicity causes increased automaticity with impaired conduction: frequent ventricular ectopics, bigeminy, atrial tachycardia with block, accelerated junctional rhythm, bidirectional VT and AV block. Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalaemia, and Osborn (J) waves suggest hypothermia.

oldText: Digoxin Fab reverses toxicity. Strongest distractor: Calcium was historically cautioned.
newText: Bidirectional VT (alternating QRS axis beat to beat) is highly characteristic of digoxin toxicity (also catecholaminergic polymorphic VT and aconite poisoning). Treat with digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab), dosed by the ingested dose or serum level, or empirically (for example 5–10 vials in acute toxicity); indications include life-threatening arrhythmias, potassium above 5–6 mmol/L in acute toxicity, and end-organ dysfunction. Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia. DC cardioversion in digoxin toxicity can precipitate refractory VF, so use the lowest energy if unavoidable. The old warning against IV calcium is now doubted, but it is not a treatment.

oldText: Unstable rhythms require cardioversion. Strongest distractor: Drugs are for stable patients.
newText: New AF with rapid ventricular response causing haemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock, ischaemic chest pain, acute heart failure or reduced consciousness) needs immediate synchronised DC cardioversion, typically starting at about 120–200 J biphasic (ERC suggests maximum energy), with sedation if the patient is conscious and heparin given without delaying cardioversion. Amiodarone is used if cardioversion fails or AF recurs, or for rate control in unstable patients with heart failure. Anticoagulation alone and digoxin act too slowly.
